title: Tokens, Vectors, and Transformers · Level 1
slo: Explain how text is prepared and represented for a transformer model.

exercises.question_text: Which statements about token IDs are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A token ID is an integer
options.rationale: A token ID is a unique integer. It identifies a vocabulary token.

options.text: Each distinct vocabulary token has an ID
options.rationale: Vocabulary entries receive identifiers. These IDs distinguish distinct tokens.

options.text: A repeated token keeps its ID
options.rationale: The ID belongs to the vocabulary token. Repeating that token does not create a new ID.
An ID identifies which token appears. Position identifies where an occurrence appears.
options.better_fit: Use positional encoding to show sequence location.

exercises.explanation: Correct. IDs identify vocabulary tokens rather than their locations.

exercises.question_text: What is a vector in this context?

options.rationale: A vector contains multiple numeric values. Its individual values are dimensions.
A token ID is one integer. A vector is an array containing multiple values.
options.better_fit: Use this to identify a distinct vocabulary token.

options.rationale: Location in a sequence is positional information. A vector is a numeric representation.
options.better_fit: Use this when recording where a token occurs.

options.rationale: A predicted token is a generation result. A vector represents information used in processing.
options.better_fit: Use this when describing a decoder's selected continuation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A vector is an array with multiple numeric dimensions.

exercises.question_text: If "a" appears twice, both occurrences use the same token ID.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A repeated token would incorrectly become a new vocabulary entry.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: IDs identify token identity, while positional encoding distinguishes occurrences.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Repeating a vocabulary token does not create another ID.

exercises.question_text: A token vector is a single unique integer used to identify a token.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The token's representation would be mistaken for its identifier.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A vector contains multiple numeric values; a token ID is one integer.

exercises.explanation: Correct. That describes a token ID, not a vector.

exercises.question_text: Which statements about initial vectors and position are correct? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: Initial vectors are randomly assigned before becoming embeddings. They are later transformed through processing.

options.text: Position tells where a token occurs
options.rationale: Positional encoding supplies a token occurrence's location. This provides order information.
Changing order changes how tokens relate. Positional encoding helps preserve that distinction.

options.text: Each occurrence needs a new token ID
options.rationale: Repeated tokens retain their vocabulary ID. Different positions distinguish their occurrences.
options.better_fit: Use a new ID for a genuinely distinct vocabulary token.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Initial vectors begin randomly and position preserves meaningful order.

exercises.question_text: What does a transformer model do?

options.text: Transforms representations and predicts next tokens
options.rationale: A transformer creates embeddings from token representations and predicts probable next tokens. Its architecture includes encoder and decoder components.
Assigning IDs occurs during tokenization. A transformer performs representation and prediction work.
options.better_fit: Use this while preparing vocabulary tokens.

options.rationale: Position information indicates order. A transformer uses representations to create embeddings and make predictions.
options.better_fit: Use this when supplying sequence-location information.

options.rationale: Instructions can establish response behavior or tone. They are not the transformer architecture.
options.better_fit: Use this for a system instruction that guides style.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A transformer creates contextual representations and predicts likely next tokens.

exercises.question_text: The same token can keep one token ID while appearing at different positions.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A repeated token would be treated as new simply because it appeared later.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The ID identifies the token; positional encoding shows its occurrence location.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Token identity and sequence location are separate.

exercises.question_text: A transformer has only an encoder block and no decoder layer.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The architecture's prediction component would be omitted.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The encoder creates embeddings, while the decoder predicts probable next tokens.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A transformer includes both an encoder block and a decoder layer.

options.text: Breaking text into tokens and assigning IDs
options.rationale: Tokenization separates text into distinct tokens and assigns identifiers. This prepares language for model processing.
Embeddings are contextual representations created after token preparation. They do not split text into tokens.
options.better_fit: Use this for encoder processing that creates contextual representations.

options.rationale: Position information identifies where an occurrence appears. It does not determine the token pieces.
options.better_fit: Use this when sequence order must be represented.

options.rationale: Next-token prediction generates a likely continuation. Tokenization prepares the input first.
options.better_fit: Use this for decoder output generation.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Tokenization prepares text as identifiable tokens.

exercises.question_text: Which statements correctly match transformer blocks to their work? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: The encoder creates contextual embeddings. It applies attention to token vectors.
The decoder uses embeddings to predict the next probable token. This supports sequential generation.
Attention is applied in the encoder. It helps produce a strong vector representation.
Token IDs are assigned during tokenization. The decoder uses representations and prediction components instead.
options.better_fit: Use this while creating identifiers for vocabulary tokens.

exercises.explanation: Correct. The encoder creates embeddings and the decoder predicts probable tokens.

exercises.question_text: Tokenization breaks text only into complete words, never sub-words or punctuation.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: That choice would exclude valid token types.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Tokenization may use words, sub-words, punctuation, and other common character sequences.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Tokens can include sub-words and punctuation.

exercises.question_text: The decoder uses embeddings, attention, and a feed-forward neural network to predict the next most probable token.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The prediction process would omit components used to choose a continuation.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The decoder uses embeddings, attention, and a feed-forward neural network to predict a likely next token.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Those components support the decoder's next-token prediction.

flashcards.back: It breaks text into tokens and assigns each token an ID.
A unique integer that identifies a token in the vocabulary.
Information that tells the model where a token appears in a sequence.
It creates embeddings from token vectors using attention.
